beginner.headline: Waymo Stops US Freeway Taxi Trips for Now
beginner.brief: Waymo has stopped its driverless taxis from using US freeways for now. Driverless taxis carry passengers without a human driver. Freeways are large roads for fast traffic. California banned the taxis from its freeways after several traffic problems. Some Waymo cars entered areas where people were working on the road. California officials said the cars were a danger to people in these areas. Waymo said there were no reports of anyone being hurt in the incident near San Francisco. Waymo said it was working with state officials to start freeway trips again. The taxis can still carry passengers on normal city streets.

intermediate.headline: Waymo Pauses Driverless Taxi Services on US Freeways
intermediate.brief: Waymo has temporarily suspended freeway services for its driverless taxis across the United States. The decision followed a California ban after a series of traffic incidents involving the company's vehicles. California officials said the taxis created a safety risk by repeatedly entering construction zones where people were working. In one incident, several Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101. Waymo said no injuries or collisions were reported after the incident on US Route 101. In another incident, video appeared to show a Waymo car trying to pass vehicles that were deliberately slowing traffic. California's ban took effect on 11 November. The restrictions will remain until Waymo shows state officials it has taken effective steps to deal with the problems. Waymo said it also paused freeway services in its other markets to evaluate how its vehicles were performing. The company said it was working with state officials to resume freeway services. Its driverless taxis can still operate on regular city streets.

advanced.headline: Waymo Pauses US Freeway Services After California Ban
advanced.brief: Waymo has announced a temporary withdrawal of its driverless taxis from freeways throughout the United States. The nationwide decision followed California's prohibition on freeway operations after several traffic incidents. In imposing the ban, California's Department of Motor Vehicles described an “imminent hazard to public safety” and pointed to several Waymo vehicles entering an active construction area on US Route 101. The regulator identified recurring incursions into active construction areas as a safety risk, noting the presence of workers, vehicles and equipment. Waymo said that no injuries or collisions had been reported following the Route 101 incident south of San Francisco. Separate footage circulating widely on social media appeared to show one of its cars attempting to overtake patrol vehicles while they intentionally slowed highway traffic in San Francisco. California's ban took effect on 11 November, with its removal contingent on Waymo demonstrating effective corrective action to address the deficiencies that precipitated it. Waymo said its broader freeway pause was in keeping with its safety principles and was intended to allow it to assess performance in its other operating markets. The company also said it was working diligently with state officials towards restarting freeway services. Data on Waymo's website suggest that its vehicles are involved in 95% fewer crashes causing serious injury than human drivers. Although Waymo operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, freeway journeys had been available in only a few locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami. Its taxis remain permitted to operate on ordinary city streets. In May, the company recalled thousands of vehicles over a software problem that could allow them to enter flooded roads.
